content.prompt:
During Term 2, Rachel did 9 spelling tests. The tests were scored out of 20.
Her mean score is 15 and her standard deviation is 2.54.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If Rachel had scored 2 extra marks on every test,

children.label: i
children.prompt: What would happen to her mean?

answer.worked: $15+2=17$. Her mean increases by 2 marks to 17.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Explain why her standard deviation would be unchanged.

answer.short: The spread of the distribution has not changed.
answer.worked: Every score and the mean increase by 2 marks, so each score's distance from the mean stays the same. The standard deviation remains 2.54.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If Rachel had scored 15 on every test,

children.label: i
children.prompt: What would happen to her mean?

answer.worked: All 9 scores would be 15, so their mean would still be 15.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Explain why her standard deviation would be zero.

answer.short: No spread means zero standard deviation.
answer.worked: Every score equals the mean of 15, so every distance from the mean is zero. There is no spread, so the standard deviation is zero.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What will happen to Rachel’s standard deviation if she scores 15 on her next test?

answer.short: Decreases: the new score equals the mean.
answer.worked: The new score of 15 equals the existing mean, so the mean stays 15. The new score adds no squared distance from the mean, while the number of scores increases from 9 to 10. The population standard deviation decreases.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What will happen to Rachel’s standard deviation if she scores 0 on her next test?

answer.short: Increases: 0 is far below the current mean.
answer.worked: The new score of 0 is 15 marks below the current mean, much farther than the current standard deviation of 2.54. This low score increases the spread, so the standard deviation increases.

inlines.text: In a small business, the seven employees earn the following wages per week:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the population standard deviation for this set of data, rounded to the nearest dollar.

answer.worked:
Enter the seven wages in the calculator's 1-variable statistics mode and select population standard deviation $\sigma_x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_x &\approx \$191.0443906\\&\approx \$191\quad\text{(nearest dollar)}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Each employee receives a $\$20$ pay increase.
Explain the effect that this increase will have on the standard deviation.

answer.short: Unchanged; the spread of the wages is unchanged.
answer.worked: Every wage and the mean increase by $\$20$, so each wage's distance from the mean stays the same. The standard deviation is unchanged.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Instead of the $\$20$ increase, every employee receives a 10% pay rise. Calculate the new population standard deviation to the nearest dollar.

answer.worked:
Enter the new wages \$330, \$539, \$572, \$649, \$726, \$748 and \$1067 in the calculator's 1-variable statistics mode and select population standard deviation $\sigma_x$.
$$\sigma_x \approx \$210.1488296 \approx \$210\quad\text{(nearest dollar)}$$
Multiplying every wage by $1.1$ also multiplies the standard deviation by $1.1$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Which pay rise gives the smaller standard deviation: $\$20$ each or 10% each?

answer.worked: The $\$20$ pay rise leaves the standard deviation at approximately $\$191$. The 10% pay rise increases it to approximately $\$210$, so $\$20$ each gives the smaller standard deviation.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy review · High priority · unsupported-transition · pf-b1e8f00cb5]
Finding: Predicting the effect of adding a score equal to the mean requires a relationship that preceding teaching has not explained.
Breakdown: Students know how to calculate population standard deviation from complete datasets, but Rachel’s individual scores are unavailable. Adding her mean leaves the mean and extremes unchanged while reducing standard deviation. The qualitative descriptions of spread do not resolve this distinction.
Checked: All supplied teaching and practice preceding Q4 were checked. Q1(j–k) provides a useful numerical precursor by removing the mean, but does not identify that feature or explain its effect. Q3(f) changes the frequency of an extreme value. Neither supplies the relationship needed for Q4(c). Q4(d) is adequately supported by the qualitative teaching: zero is far from Rachel’s mean relative to her existing spread, so that target is excluded.
Assumes: The supplied teaching is complete. Students use the calculator methods explicitly taught; no prior rule about adding observations is assumed.
Proposed repair (add-cue): Before Q4(c), add: 'Compare Q1(j) and (k). Part (k) removes −1.5, the mean of both datasets, and the population standard deviation increases. Reversing this change shows that adding a score equal to the existing mean decreases population standard deviation.'
Done when: Students have an explicit connection between the earlier numerical comparison and adding a score at the mean before answering Q4(c).

entries.description:
Standard Deviation
Standard deviation is a number that describes how far data is spread from the mean.
It measures the ‘average’ distance of each data value from the mean using a special formula.
A larger standard deviation means more spread in the data.
A lower standard deviation means less spread and more consistency.
